Extract A: 1914- 2014 
As of 2014, it is 100 years since the first real global conflict - World War 1. It began in 1914 
and was concluded in 1918. Millions died on the battlefields of Europe as Germany and its 
allies fought a four-year trench warfare against the Allies led by Great Britain. Many 
countries were aligned with Great Britain, particularly the Commonwealth countries, 
including Australia, New Zealand, Canada, India and South Africa. This was a great 
patriotic war and these countries were involved in the conflict early in 1914. 
At the time of the outbreak of hostilities the British Government requested Australia's 
assistance in men and materials. Just north of Australia lay Papua New Guinea. This area 
was then German New Guinea. In this area there were a number of radio communication 
stations. Their existence meant that German New Guinea would be in contact with the 
powerful German fleet. The British Government wanted to isolate the area, so that no 
information could pass from it to the German Fleet. 
On 9 August a request was made for Australia to take on this task. The orders were simple 
- a small contingent would need to be sent to destroy the radio communication centres in 
German New Guinea, and another group would bolster the small force of troops on 
Thursday Island, just south of the German territory. 
The first group, the Australian Naval and Military Expeditionary Force, was made up of 
1,500 volunteers. The objective in destroying the radio communication towers was 
completed in September of 1914. This was the first action of Australian troops in the 
Pacific region, and it effectively isolated the German colony from contact with Berlin or the 
German fleet. The group that was sent to Thursday Island spent much of their time 
managing the fort and patrolling the island. Within a few months there was not even the 
remote possibility of Australia being invaded from the north, and the troops were 
withdrawn. Australia had played a small but significant role in protecting our shores.

Extract B: Closing In - Marines in the Seizure of lwo Jima 
Sunday, 4 March 1945, marked the end of the second week of the U.S. invasion of lwo 
Jima. By this point the assault elements of the 3d, 4th, and 5th Marine Divisions were 
exhausted, their combat efficiency reduced to dangerously low levels. The thrilling sight of 
the American flag being raised by the 28th Marines on Mount Suribachi had occurred 10 
days earlier, a lifetime on "Sulphur Island." The landing forces of the V Amphibious Corps 
(VAC) had already sustained 13,000 casualties, including 3,000 dead. The "front lines" .. ,- •··--... - . 'I ~ M·•~ • ! 
were a jagged::serration across lwo's fat northern half, still in the middle of the main 
Japanese defences. Ahead the going seemed all uphill against a well-disciplined, rarely 
visible enemy.

Questions 23 to 28. 
The Shopping Trolley 
It might be the humblest proof of how far everyday technology has come: the shopping 
trolley. Simple, sturdy and so ordinary we barely notice it, yet in 1937 it was a revelation. In 
Oklahoma City, supermarket owner Sylvan N. Goldman looked at a folding chair in his 
office and wondered what would happen if he put wheels on it and added baskets. With 
mechanic Fred Young, he built a metal frame that held wire baskets and rolled it into his 
Humpty Dumpty stores. For a moment, it looked as if retail history would yawn and walk 
past. 
23 . Goldman tried newspaper ads that promised a new, easier way to shop, but 
the idea still stalled. So he hired men and women to stroll the aisles with trolleys and to 
show how natural it felt to use one. The tactic worked, confidence grew, and the wheeled 
basket moved from curiosity to convenience. Goldman's spark did not appear out of thin 
air. Self-service shopping had been spreading since 1916, when Clarence Saunders 
opened Piggly Wiggly in Memphis and invited customers to help themselves from open 
shelves. 24 . The trolley solved a practical problem created by self-service: it let 
people gather more goods without running out of arms or patience. 
Goldman moved quickly to protect and refine the concept. He filed for patents on a 
collapsible, wheeled carrier that could hold stacked baskets and be folded for storage. A 
key patent was granted in April 1940 for what he called a folding basket carriage for self- 
service stores. 25 . Another inventor, Orla Watson of Kansas City, supplied the 
breakthrough that made trolleys practical for store layouts. In 1946 he designed a single, 
full basket trolley with a swinging rear gate that allowed one cart to nest inside another. 
After a patent dispute, Goldman relinquished his competing claim and Watson received the 
crucial patent in 1949. That nesting line you see by the doors is a direct descendant of 
Watson's design. 
From there, the trolley became a day to day part of modern consumer life. 26 _ 
Histories of supermarkets often point to the mid twentieth century as the era when the self­ 
serve model, the family car and the trolley reinforced one another, turning the big weekly 
shop into a routine that shaped suburban life. The evolution had not stopped at wire and 
wheels. From the late twentieth century onward, the trolley began to shape how we shop 
as much as it served us. Researchers tested how cart size and layout influenced 
behaviour. 27 . Other trials show that dividing a cart into sections can nudge 
people to load more fruit and vegetables, lifting healthy purchases substantially. 
Behind the scenes, the humble frame keeps evolving for safety and control. European 
makers such as Wanzl helped standardise features like coin-deposit locks, while third 
parties introduce safety specifications such as ASTM F2372 to set performance 
requirements for child seating and restraint systems. 28 . Today, manufacturers 
talk about scan-as-you-shop setups, app integrations and smarter gates at exits, all aimed 
at saving minutes and smoothing the path from shelf to boot. 
So yes, it is just a trolley. Yet tucked inside its quiet clatter are ideas about convenience, 
persuasion and scale. It began as a folding chair on castors, mocked by some and ignored 
by many. It became a cultural fixture not by shock value, but through patient design, canny 
marketing and a knack for timing. A metal basket on wheels, nudging the twentieth century, 
and the rest of us, a few steps further down the aisle.

Extract A 
The Great Barrier Reef stretches for 2000 kilometres along the Queensland coast. It is not 
only the largest coral reef complex in the world, but it is the biggest construction of any 
kind made by living animals; nothing made by humans comes close to being as large and 
extensive. Approximately 2500 separate reefs make up the Great Barrier Reef; combined 
they would cover an area twice the size of England. 
The structures of the Great Barrier Reef have been built by countless millions of minute 
animals called 'polyps'. Each of these minute, soft-bodied animals builds an exceedingly 
small, cup-like home of corallite (lime) to live in and to give it support and protection. These 
limestone apartments are joined together in huge clusters like blocks of flats - sometimes 
tall and pointed, and sometimes low and spreading. 
To thrive, coral polyps need a constant environment of warm water that is clear and 
shallow with enough movement to carry plankton, the even-smaller floating animal food, to 
the non-moving polyps. The shallow continental shelf off the Queensland coast, 
particularly along the outer edge, provides ideal conditions for the tiny coral animals.
